To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the capacity to attack a stranger is highly heritable and genetically correlated with the GAD activity of the olfactory bulbs; (2) the Y chromosome does not influence the two phenotypes; (3) males of more aggressive strains have a lower sensitivity to odours, which makes the olfactory discrimination and recognition of the intruder easier and more efficient.
inter-male aggression and GAD activity in olfactory bulb are inversely correlated, and that Y chromosome effect is not involved in this association.

intermale aggression and olfactory bulb gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) activity are negatively correlated and that the non-pseudoautosomal region of the sex chromosome (YNPAR) is not involved in this correlation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic control of aggression and olfactory function in mice.
the study of the genetic basis of aggressive behavior and its relation to other traits, such as olfactory sensitivity.
the study of the genetic bases of the aggressiveness and the GABAergic activity of the olfactory bulbs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the YNPAR has a minor effect on intermale aggression in mice.
a higher GAD activity in olfactory bulbs is associated with a higher aggressiveness, and that the non-pseudo-autosomal region of the Y chromosome is not involved.
the YNPAR of the mouse is not involved in the intermale aggressive behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the olfactory system plays a role in the control of aggression and that the YNPAR has no effect on the olfactory system or on aggression.
the olfactory bulbs play a key role in the regulation of intermale aggression.
intermale aggression and olfactory bulb GAD activity are two different aspects of the same phenomenon, namely the ability to identify a stranger, and this ability is under genetic control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the olfactory bulbs are involved in intermale aggression in mice.
the genetic background of the mouse strain, and not the YNPAR, determines the level of intermale aggression and the activity of GAD in the olfactory bulb.
